title: Primary Function of the Shaft
learningObjectives: Identify the shaft's role in the drive system.
student: State the primary structural function of shaft AB.
instructor: The shaft transmits mechanical power and torque from the motor to the pulley and downstream driven equipment.

title: Power Input and Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Relate operating power and speed to torque.
student: Identify the operating quantities that create the shaft loading.
instructor: Motor power P and angular speed ω determine the transmitted torque through P = Tω.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish radial support from torsional restraint.
student: Identify the role of the motor connection at A and the bearing at B.
instructor: The motor-side coupling applies torque at A. The bearing supports the shaft radially while permitting rotation and is not treated as a torsional restraint in the base model.

title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque through the drive components.
student: Trace the torque path from the motor to the driven equipment.
instructor: The path is motor rotor, coupling at A, shaft AB, pulley, belts, and downstream machine.

title: Critical Component and Response
student: Identify the critical component and mechanical response in the base problem.
instructor: The solid steel shaft is the critical component, and its maximum torsional shear stress occurs at the outer surface.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify inputs controlling torque and stress.
student: List the parameters controlling shaft stress and explain their roles.
instructor: Power and speed determine torque; torque and diameter determine shear stress; allowable stress sets the design limit. For a solid shaft, τmax varies with T/d3.

title: Speed Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Predict how lower speed affects torque and shaft size.
student: For fixed motor power, predict what happens to torque and required diameter if shaft speed decreases.
instructor: Torque increases because T = P/ω. Required diameter also increases, with dmin proportional to T1/3.

title: Student-Generated Torsion Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a torsion model before viewing the reference figure.
student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified torsion model of the motor, shaft, pulley, and bearing. Show applied torque, diameter, and rotational direction.
instructor: A valid model treats AB as a uniform solid circular shaft carrying constant internal torque between the motor and pulley, with B shown as a rotation-permitting bearing.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the torsion model before seeing the instructor idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the torsion equations.
student: State the assumptions used in the base analysis.
instructor: Assume steady operation, a uniform solid circular shaft, linear elasticity, pure torsion, constant transmitted power, negligible bearing friction, and no belt bending, keyway, stress concentration, shock, or fatigue effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete stress-based shaft selection.
student: Outline the calculation sequence before substituting numbers.
instructor: Convert rpm to rad/s; compute torque from power; solve the solid-shaft stress equation for minimum diameter; round upward to the available increment; verify selected-size stress; then evaluate twist if required.

title: Torsion Boundary Conditions
student: From the reference diagram, identify the torsion-related boundary conditions and idealizations.
instructor: Torque enters at A from the motor and is removed at the pulley. Bearing B supports the shaft radially but permits rotation and does not remove transmitted torque in this idealization.

title: Angular Speed
learningObjectives: Convert rotational speed to angular speed.
student: Convert the assigned shaft speed from rpm to rad/s.

title: Transmitted Torque
learningObjectives: Calculate torque from motor power and speed.
student: Determine the torque carried by the shaft from the specified motor power and speed.
commonMistakes: Do not mix lb-ft torque with a diameter measured in inches.

title: Internal Torque Diagram
learningObjectives: Determine the shaft's internal torque distribution.
student: Draw and label the internal torque diagram for shaft AB.
instructor: The internal torque is constant over the power-transmitting shaft segment and has magnitude {{shaft_torque_lb_ft}} lb·ft.

title: Minimum Theoretical Diameter
learningObjectives: Solve the solid-shaft torsion equation for diameter.
student: Using the allowable shear stress, determine the minimum theoretical diameter of the solid circular shaft.

title: Standard Shaft Selection
learningObjectives: Select a manufacturable diameter without violating stress.
student: Select the smallest available shaft diameter using the assigned standard-size increment. Explain the rounding direction.
instructor: Round upward to {{shaft_d_selected_label}}. The selected decimal diameter is {{shaft_d_selected_in}} in; the next lower available size is {{shaft_d_lower_in}} in and does not meet the theoretical minimum.

title: Selected-Diameter Verification
learningObjectives: Verify stress and quantify design margin.
student: Calculate the actual maximum shear stress, utilization ratio, and allowable-stress factor for the selected shaft.
instructor: τactual = {{shaft_tau_actual_ksi}} ksi. Utilization is {{shaft_utilization}}, and the allowable-stress factor is {{shaft_allowable_factor}}. {{shaft_stress_assessment}}

title: Angle-of-Twist Check
learningObjectives: Calculate polar moment and shaft twist.
student: For the assigned shaft length and shear modulus, calculate the polar moment and angle of twist, then compare the result with the twist limit.

title: Engineering Assessment
student: State whether the selected shaft is acceptable in the base model and identify omitted checks required for detailed design.
instructor:
{{shaft_recommendation}}

Detailed design must also consider belt-induced bending, bearing reactions, keyways and stress concentrations, fatigue, shock loading, critical speed, coupling details, and manufacturing tolerances.
gradingNotes: Students should not claim full system safety from the pure-torsion calculation alone.
